👋 Hi! I’m Xinyi Yi, a PhD student in Engineering at the University of Cambridge, Churchill College.
My research focuses on the optimal control and coordination of multi-energy systems, with a current emphasis on district heating networks, energy sharing, and data-driven temperature regulation.
I am currently supervised by Prof. Ioannis Lestas.
During my master’s at Tsinghua University, I worked under the guidance of Prof. Ye Guo, and during my undergraduate studies at North China Electric Power University, I was jointly advised by Prof. Cheng Yu and Prof. Ming Zhou.

content:
🎉 Our paper “Optimal Energy-sharing and Temperature Regulation in District Heating Systems” has been accepted to NECsys 2025, to be held in Hong Kong, June 2–5, 2025.
📘 Abstract We consider the problem of temperature regulation and optimal energy sharing in district heating systems without requiring any knowledge of the demand, while ensuring satisfactory transient performance.
We show that convex optimization problems can be formulated to jointly achieve optimal temperature regulation and energy sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LQR formulations can asymptotically converge to these optimal operating points—while also minimizing transient performance metrics.
The effectiveness of our approach is validated through comprehensive simulation studies.

content:
🎯 A Closed-loop Vision: From Markets to Control and Back My research explores how distributed control mechanisms can support real-world operation and pricing in multi-energy systems. I aim to bridge physical dynamics with market coordination, especially across electricity and heat sectors.
🔍 From Market Design to System Control My academic journey began with the study of multi-energy system scheduling and market-based pricing mechanisms, particularly in electricity and district heating systems. During my undergraduate and master’s training, I focused on how coordinated optimization of electricity and heat flows could support more efficient and equitable energy market pricing, including energy and reserve markets.
In my PhD, I shifted focus toward system control theory, especially on the shorter time scale of ancillary services such as frequency regulation. My current research emphasizes the co-regulation of frequency and temperature using methods such as energy-sharing controllers, LQR formulations, and Port-Hamiltonian modeling.
While I am currently focused on building robust technical foundations, I ultimately aim to return to the market layer, enabling physically sound yet economically aligned control strategies. My long-term goal is to enable control algorithms that can directly interact with market mechanisms, completing a loop from market design → distributed control → market integration.
From economic coordination to distributed control — and back again.
🔌 Coupled Electric–Thermal Control I design controllers that co-regulate power system frequency and thermal system temperature in combined heat and power (CHP) networks, including:
Secondary frequency control via PH systems Energy-sharing temperature regulation Heat pump integration and transient-aware feedback 📊 Energy Sharing under Uncertainty My recent work investigates steady-state and transient temperature control without demand forecasts:
Convex steady-state problem formulation Demand-independent energy-sharing regulators Theoretical guarantees on convergence and performance 🧠 Data-driven Temperature Regulation To enable adaptivity and deployment, I explore learning-based control strategies:
LQR with unknown dynamics Policy iteration with stability Learning-based control of pipeline networks 🔁 Long-term Vision My future work aims to close the loop between system control and market mechanisms, by:
Embedding control objectives into market clearing Designing control-compatible pricing models Enabling distributed participation in ancillary markets Bridging real-world control and energy markets.
